 Pinned Jess Bidgood and Catie Edmondson 
 Here’s the latest. 
 A new political era opened in Washington on Wednesday, as Democrats vowed to use their sweeping majority to check President Trump’s power, while prominent Republicans blamed their midterm wipeout on his agenda and party leadership.
 Democrats were on track to secure at least a 50-seat majority in the House and solid control of the Senate after notching seismic victories around the country, in deep red House districts and long-Republican Senate seats. Vice President JD Vance blamed the rout on Mr. Trump’s decision to start a war with Iran, a remarkable break from a president who, for much of the past decade, has demanded total fealty from his party.
 “Everyone knows why we lost,” Mr. Vance said on social media. For his part, Mr. Trump said Mr. Vance’s assessment was “largely true.” He added, “If I had to do it again, I’d have to do it again.”
 Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the minority leader who is expected to become the first Black speaker of the House, predicted Democrats would win at least 255 of the 435 seats in the chamber, comparing the scope of his party’s romp to an “American tsunami.” Democrats picked off Republicans who had not expected competitive races in conservative-leaning seats from Indiana to Missouri to Alabama, putting themselves on pace to make generational gains similar to those of the Republican wave of 1994 — only in reverse.
 After two years of Republican control of Congress that reduced the House’s role to that of mere bystander, Mr. Jeffries promised to reassert the chamber’s power by undertaking aggressive investigations with oversight.
 “The days of the House of Representatives functioning like a wholly owned subsidiary of the Trump administration are over,” Mr. Jeffries promised.
 Republicans lost Senate seats in Maine , Iowa , Kansas , Ohio , North Carolina , South Carolina and even Texas , according to The Associated Press. Two other tight Senate contests haven’t been called: Ballots were still being counted in Alaska’s contentious Senate race and in the unlikely battleground of Mississippi , where roughly 1,100 votes separated the two candidates as of Wednesday evening.
 The decisive control of the Senate is a “generational remake,” Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic leader, told reporters in Washington.
 Voters across every major demographic group — race, age, gender and education — made a drastic swing left in Tuesday’s election, reversing the gains Mr. Trump had made with them in 2024.
 Mr. Trump seemed to brush off the sweeping repudiation. He used his first public appearance on Wednesday to tour the site of the ballroom he is building on the White House grounds. There, he defended what he considered to be his legacy-defining projects. “It’s going to be not only one of the biggest, but it’ll be the most beautiful ballroom, I think, anywhere in the world,” he said.
 The shock waves from the election reverberated more resoundingly among other Republicans, who had feared widespread losses but had not anticipated such a renunciation of their party.
 Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana told aides that he would not seek to lead the House G.O.P. conference in the minority, setting off a scramble among ambitious Republicans to succeed him. Representative Jim Jordan of Ohio announced he would seek the role, arguing that Republicans needed to take a combative approach toward the Democratic majority next year.
 “In these next two years, our job cannot be merely to spotlight how radical this new Democrat party is,” he said. “Offense, not defense, wins elections.”
 Representative Steve Scalise of Louisiana also jumped into the contest, arguing that Republicans must act with more unity.
 Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida said his fellow Republicans in Washington should have voted to release the Epstein files earlier and banned congressional stock trading. He called the election as “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans in many parts of the country as we have seen probably in the last 100 years.”
 Mr. Trump told The New York Times in an interview late Tuesday night that he was “absolutely willing to accept” the midterm results and was prepared to work with Democrats — despite his repeated efforts to sow doubts about voter fraud and to have the Justice Department intervene in elections.
 Here’s what else we’re covering:
 Democratic landslide: The Democrats’ landslide did not just reach the federal races but also state and local governments. The party notched firsts in governors’ races and won down-ballot races like those for state treasurer, secretary of state and state legislature. Democrats are set to be in the majority in a dozen statehouse chambers where they had been the minority party. 
 G.O.P. bright spots: Republicans fended off a significant challenge in a Senate race in Florida, with Senator Ashley Moody defeating Angie Nixon, a progressive Democrat. Byron Donalds , a staunch Trump supporter, was elected Florida’s first Black governor, keeping the Republicans’ hold on that office.
 Ballot measures: Voters across the country also weighed in on a range of statewide issues, including abortion, how future elections would be run and how their own votes would be counted. Read more ›

 Reporting from Alaska Teresa Benitez-Thompson, a Democrat and former state legislator, defeated David Flippo, an Air Force veteran and financial adviser, according to The Associated Press, to win the open seat in Nevada’s open Second Congressional District, a conservative region in the northern part of the state.
 The district has never been represented by a Democrat, but Flippo was plagued by a series of scandals related to his finances and accusations of stolen military valor, with even the district’s retiring Republican incumbent, Representative Mark Amodei, saying he would not vote for him.

 These Republicans bet big on Trump. It didn’t pay off. 
 Clockwise from top left: Senator Darline Graham of South Carolina; Michael Whatley of North Carolina; Attorney General Ken Paxton of Texas; and Senator Jon Husted of Ohio. The New York Times President Trump used to gloat about his near-perfect endorsement record, reveling in the control he exerted over the Republican nomination process during this year’s primary season. Voters overwhelmingly rewarded the candidates he backed and punished those who displeased him, muscling numerous less loyal candidates out of contention.
 “If you pushed back” on Mr. Trump, said Justin Evans, a Republican strategist in South Carolina, “you’d get your head chopped off.”
 Mr. Trump has little to brag about this week. Senate candidates he had helped elevate, including Darline Graham in South Carolina, Michael Whatley in North Carolina and Ken Paxton in Texas, lost by margins previously unimagined by even the most optimistic Democrats. Those high-profile defeats contributed to what Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida, a one-time Trump rival for the presidential nomination, called as “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans” as the country has seen in a century.
 “The people who did the best last night were the people who distanced themselves from the president,” Mr. Evans said, calling the results “a universal repudiation of the bullying that’s been taking place during this primary” by Mr. Trump.
 Here’s a look at what happened to some of the candidates who tied their fortunes most closely to Mr. Trump.
 Darline Graham
 Image President Trump with Darline Graham during a rally last month. Credit... Doug Mills/The New York Times After Senator Lindsey Graham, a Republican, died in July, Mr. Trump threw his weight behind Mr. Graham’s sister, Darline Graham, in a snap primary election. While many Republican insiders objected, primary voters listened, narrowly nominating Ms. Graham over Representative Ralph Norman, despite her self-described lack of experience or policy expertise.
 On Tuesday, the wider South Carolina electorate rejected Ms. Graham , choosing to send a Democrat to Washington for the first time in nearly 30 years.
 “It wasn’t that voters rebuked Trump,” Mr. Evans said, noting that the Republican nominee for governor had earned at least 90,000 more votes than Ms. Graham. “It was that the entire Washington machine pushed this woman on South Carolina, and South Carolina resoundingly pushed back.”
 Ken Paxton
 Senate Republicans begged Mr. Trump to endorse Senator John Cornyn over Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general, in the state’s Republican Senate primary. Many argued that Mr. Paxton’s scandal-ridden past would make it significantly more difficult, and more costly, to win in a general election. They also said a contentious intraparty battle would waste resources needed in more competitive states. Mr. Trump ignored them, waiting until days before a May primary runoff to back Mr. Paxton.
 On Tuesday, despite dramatically outspending Democrats, Republicans lost the Senate seat, the governor’s mansion, and every other statewide race in Texas, breaking a more than three-decade-long streak of G.O.P. dominance.
 Some Texas Republicans speculated that Mr. Paxton would have won the primary regardless of Mr. Trump’s choice. It is also not clear that Mr. Cornyn could have defied the tsunami of voter anger that propelled Democrats to victory up and down the ballot. But some blamed Mr. Paxton, and Mr. Trump, for the extent of the losses.
 “You stand by Trump at your own peril at this point,” said Dade Phelan, the former Republican speaker of the State House. He recalled how Mr. Trump asked voters in Texas and elsewhere to “pretend I’m on the ballot.”
 “Well, voters imagined he was on the ballot,” Mr. Phelan said. “And it was an absolute apocalypse for Republicans.”
 Michael Whatley
 Mr. Trump’s fingerprints were all over North Carolina’s Senate race. First, Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican who has served in North Carolina for more than a decade, announced he would retire rather than run for re-election after the president threatened to back a primary opponent against him.
 Then, Mr. Trump handpicked Michael Whatley , a former Republican National Committee chairman, and Mr. Whatley spent millions touting Mr. Trump’s endorsement ahead of his victory in the Republican Senate primary. On Tuesday night, Mr. Whatley fell to former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper , a Democrat, by around 20 points, a stunning leftward shift for a state that Mr. Trump won in 2024.
 Meghan McMichael, 33, a voter in Canton, N.C., said on Tuesday that she had voted for Mr. Cooper and other Democrats in order to hold the Trump administration accountable for its treatment of immigrants, and the state of the economy.
 “I’m just hopeful that certain people will be held accountable for things that have happened over the last two years,” she said.
 Jon Husted
 Image Senator Jon Husted with Mr. Trump at a rally in Chillicothe, Ohio, last month. Credit... Alex Kent/The New York Times Senator Jon Husted, Ohio’s Republican Senate nominee and a former professional football player, was little known nationally until President Trump started talking about his rear end while on the campaign trail. Mr. Husted also joined Mr. Trump at several Ohio rallies in the final weeks of the campaign, tying himself to the president.
 Mr. Husted lost to former Senator Sherrod Brown on Tuesday , making Ohio one of seven states that Democrats had flipped as of Wednesday evening.
 The president’s comments about Mr. Husted’s backside may also have backfired, with voters across the country telling The New York Times they had disapproved of his remarks that Mr. Husted had a “great ass” and a “pile of muscle.”
 In Lincoln, Neb., on Tuesday, Deondre Webster, 36, said he didn’t believe Mr. Trump is a good role model for his three daughters.
 “We don’t want to see the leader of the country talking about male behinds or stuff like that onstage,” he said. “When he’s supposed to be the leader, and that’s not what we’re teaching our kids.”
 Mark Barrett in North Carolina and Justin Diep in Nebraska contributed reporting.

 Reporting from Washington “It’s so dark outside,” President Trump just wrote on social media. He wasn’t talking about the midterms, but a failed legislative effort to make daylight saving time permanent , which would have ended the semiannual time change that shortens winter days.
 Continuing his effort to shrug off an overwhelming Republican defeat in Tuesday’s elections, Trump complained that the Senate had not passed the measure by Election Day, and that the clock change back to standard time had moved the sunset in Washington today to 5:06 p.m.
 “Just a few days ago it was so nice and sunny at this same time,” Trump said in a post at 6:33 p.m., adding that “I didn’t want to make a big deal out of this prior to the Election because I didn’t want to have certain Senators lose their Race, in a landslide, but it is too bad they can’t get it done.”
 He conceded that the country has “far bigger priorities” than making daylight saving time permanent, but added, “I will keep fighting for this!”

 Reporting from Iowa Many Republicans tied their fates to President Trump, only to suffer a rude awakening on Tuesday night. That included Mayes Middleton, the Republican nominee for Texas attorney general, who spent millions from his personal fortune to brand himself as “MAGA Mayes” during a Republican primary he ultimately won over Representative Chip Roy, an established Republican and former assistant attorney general, whom he branded as anti-Trump.
 But Middleton lost soundly to a Democrat, Nathan Johnson, on Tuesday despite outspending him by more than six to one. In an interview, Johnson said he was “delighted when Mayes Middleton nicknamed himself ‘MAGA Mayes,’ because I saw this coming.”

 Reporting from Tennessee Mississippi’s secretary of state, Michael Watson, has mapped out the wait ahead for votes to be counted in the tight contest between Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith and Scott Colom, her Democratic challenger, who leads by 1,138 votes. There’s about 3,600 absentee-by-mail ballots that have to be received within five business days, plus an “unknown number of affidavit ballots.” Counties have until Nov. 13 to submit certified results to the state. 
 Nov. 4, 2026, 6:04 p.m. ET Caroline Soler and Christine Zhang 
 What we know, and don’t, in the Alaska and Mississippi Senate vote counts. 
 Image In Alaska, the votes reported on Election Day gave Mary Peltola a small advantage over Senator Daniel S. Sullivan, the Republican incumbent. Credit... Christopher Miller for The New York Times Control of the U.S. Senate has already been determined , with 33 of the 35 contests being called within hours of polls closing. In Alaska and Mississippi , however, no race calls have been made for the Senate and it could be quite some time until either contest is decided, even as some additional vote totals trickle out in the coming days.
 In both cases, the Democratic nominee is clinging to a slim lead, but the reasons for the lack of a call are far different.
 What We Know in the Alaska Senate Race
 Alaska’s Senate race could take days or weeks to be called. Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee, had a lead of fewer than 1,000 votes as of Wednesday afternoon, but nearly a quarter of the expected votes remain uncounted.
 The bulk of the remaining vote is in the form of mail-in ballots. Some were cast close to Election Day, while others were postmarked by Election Day and will be received in the days after. A smaller chunk of early in-person ballots are also outstanding.
 The deadline to tabulate all ballots, including provisional ballots, is Nov. 18. That is also the date that ranked-choice tabulation will begin, should neither Ms. Peltola nor Senator Daniel S. Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, cross the 50 percent threshold needed to win the election in the first round.
 While the late mail vote typically leans toward Democrats, multiple factors could undercut Ms. Peltola’s possible advantage, including how many ballots will be received and how many are from voters who did not rank additional candidates beyond their first choice. There is also the potentially confounding presence of the other two candidates on the ballot, Gerald L. Heikes and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr .
 A New York Times analysis of the available ranked-choice data pulled from each voter’s ballot shows that more than a third of voters who ranked Mr. Heikes or Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. as their first choice did not rank another candidate. That means these ballots would not count toward either Ms. Peltola or Senator Sullivan in subsequent rounds of the ranked-choice tabulation.
 What We Know in the Mississippi Senate Race
 Scott Colom, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Mississippi, had a razor-thin lead over Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, the Republican incumbent, as of Wednesday afternoon.. As of Wednesday evening, Scott Colom, the Democratic nominee in Mississippi, had a lead of roughly 1,000 votes over Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, the Republican incumbent. Because the margin is so tight, The Associated Press may not be able to make a race call until the state certifies a winner. 
 Mississippi is somewhat of an outlier in that it does not have a mechanism for automatic recounts, and has no method for a candidate to contest the election, so a court order would be required to initiate a recount.
 Nearly all of the votes have been counted in the race, but a smattering of provisional ballots — which are ballots given to those with questions about their eligibility to vote — are still waiting to be counted, as are some late-arriving mail ballots. According to Mississippi's secretary of state, there are approximately 3,600 outstanding mail ballots that could arrive in time to be counted. 
 Mississippi’s Supreme Court ruled in June that the state must accept mail-in ballots that arrive by the Tuesday after Election Day — this year, Nov. 10. And provisional ballots in the state must be tallied by that day as well. For a provisional ballot to be accepted, the voter is required to provide proper identification to elections officials, obtain a state voter ID card, or submit a religious exemption.
 Some counties in the state have said they hope to begin releasing some results of provisional ballots on Wednesday. It is currently unknown how many ballots remain uncounted statewide. Adding a layer of complexity, ballot processing and counting, which includes ruling on provisional ballots, is conducted by each county’s five-person elections commission rather than a single elections official. 
 In 2024, the state had just under 15,000 provisional ballots, of which 70 percent were accepted. In 2022, the state had about 5,700 provisional ballots, of which 75 percent were accepted.
 Evan Peng contributed reporting.

 Reporting from Washington
 A G.O.P. group says the party faces a ‘crisis-level’ loss of elected women. 
 Image Credit... Alex Kent/The New York Times A group that champions electing conservative women to public office issued a blunt warning to Republicans on Wednesday after the Democratic sweep of Congress, calling the defeats of a large number of G.O.P. women an emergency that must be addressed.
 “We are once again facing a crisis-level decline in Republican women in Congress,” Danielle Barrow, the president of Winning For Women Action Fund, an outside group dedicated to electing Republican women, said in a statement.
 Ms. Barrow sounded the alarm as Democrats were celebrating their own milestone of electing more than 100 women to the House for the first time in history.
 Republicans already have far less gender diversity in their ranks in the House, where there are currently 32 G.O.P. women (including two nonvoting delegates) — around 15 percent of their members.
 With the landslide Democratic victories that are projected to win them the largest House majority in decades, that number could potentially dip to below 20 next year, after all races are called.
 In 2018, when Republicans lost 40 seats and elected just one new G.O.P. woman to Congress, the party made a commitment to recruit and invest in female candidates, Ms. Barrow said. It worked: Two years later, 11 of the 15 seats Republicans flipped were by women.
 “But that commitment to recruiting women faded when the urgency did,” she said. “Republicans cannot only make this investment after a wipeout election and abandon it when things improve. It is time for party leaders to treat this as a permanent strategy, not a crisis response.”

 Reporting from Washington
 Democrats eye inquiries into Trump actions on energy, public land. 
 Image House Democrats had already announced probes into the Trump administration before the election over a $1 billion payout to cancel offshore wind farms. Credit... Randi Baird for The New York Times Democrats in Congress are poised to ramp up investigations into Trump administration efforts to limit renewable energy development, promote fossil fuels and mining, and open up public lands to commercial interests.
 Before the elections, House Democrats had already announced probes into some of those actions, including a $1 billion payout to cancel offshore wind farms , cuts to renewable energy investments in Puerto Rico and the shrinking of two national monuments in Utah . In other cases, they have raised allegations of corruption against officials overseeing public lands, fisheries and offshore energy development.
 But with a majority in Congress next year, they can deepen those inquiries, said Representative Jared Huffman, Democrat of California, who stands to be chairman of the House Natural Resources Committee as its current ranking member. In January, Democrats will gain power to convene hearings, call witnesses to testify under oath and go to court to compel cooperation by the executive branch. Under Republican control, Congress has not used those powers to look into the Trump administration.
 Just in the hours since the scope of the Democratic gains became clear, outside groups also began clamoring for new inquiries into steps by the administration to limit enforcement of pollution regulations and reduce the flow of federal disaster aid.
 Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, Democrat of Rhode Island, said such investigations could help deliver on his party’s campaign promises to promote affordability. The Trump administration’s efforts to purge the government of any focus on climate change have contributed to rising property insurance premiums and energy costs, Mr. Whitehouse said.
 “Democrats will work every angle to lower consumers’ energy costs, and we will demand accountability for the massive corruption wrought by Trump’s fossil-fuel donors through their climate denial fraud and corrupting dark money influence,” Mr. Whitehouse said in a statement.
 The Environmental Protection Network, a nonpartisan group of hundreds of former Environmental Protection Agency officials, called for investigations into Trump administration pollution-limit rollbacks and rule exemptions. The group said the administration has ignored scientific evidence and its own experts to put industry above public health.
